title: Bitcoin, Iran, and Millions on Polymarket: Who Knew About the War in Advance?
transcript_text: Just a few hours before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran last Saturday, six anonymous crypto wallets placed their bets on foreign markets. When the first missile hit the Iran, those bets paid off, earning $1.2 million for correctly predicting the exact day of the strike. The timing of the trade raised questions about whether the traders had access to advanced information. Proponents argue that prediction markets aren't just about gambling, but about forecasting the future, and that they can be more accurate than polls and experts. Critics, however, warn that they are dystopian experiment, riddled with insider trading, manipulation and even risks to national security. So, who is right? In this video we'll break down what prediction markets really are, how they work, who's making money, and what's at stake if they keep growing. Before we begin, don't forget to like and subscribe, so you don't miss our next video. I'm Giovanni, let's start. Prediction markets are platforms where you place a wager on a future contract, the value of which is equivalent to the probability of a specific event happening. Here is an example of how it works. Let's say there is a prediction market asking, will it rain in New York tomorrow? At the start of the day, the yes option is trading at 40 cents, which means the market think there is about a 40% chance of rain. Then a new weather report comes out, showing a storm moving in. People who see that information start buying yes shares, pushing the price up to 70 cents. Now the market is saying there is roughly a 70% chance of rain. If it actually rains, each yes share pays out $1. If it doesn't, it pays nothing. So the price moves as people react to new information and the market's prediction updates in real time. This is not a novelty as a concept, prediction markets have existed for decades. One early example was the Iowa electronic markets launched in the late 80s. Another key difference between prediction markets and traditional gambling websites is that you don't bet against the House. The platform makes money regardless of whether you win or lose. But that is not the main ground-breaking aspect of these platforms. Prediction markets are widely seen as reliable indicators of the likelihood of real-world events. The logic is simple. When people have money on the line, their predictions tend to be more accurate than traditional polls. Think about it. These numbers aren't produced by a centralized authority, like a panel of experts, a survey firm, or a media organization. They emerge from a global network of participants, all putting their own money behind what they believe will happen. Some describe this as a form of decentralized truth, a system where economic incentives push people to seek the most accurate possible prediction. That's the reason why outlets like CNN and CNBC have partnered with Kallchi to integrate prediction market data into their coverage. It seems that the Coinbase CEO doesn't see a problem with this. In his view, he was simply injecting new information into the market. Of course, these dynamic raises serious questions about fairness and user protection. Known insiders are clearly at a disadvantage and have much lower chance of making money on these platforms. But insider trading is not just a matter of customer protection. Prediction markets have been criticized for allowing people to profit from global catastrophes and tragedies. For example, in mid-November alone, there were almost a hundred million dollars at stake on markets related to the war in Ukraine. These bets are mainly on when the Russian army would capture specific towns or villages. Last year, there was even a market on Kalshi betting on whether Gaza would experience mass famine. First of all, that raises a moral issue, profiting from human suffering. People's lives are directly impacted by these events, often in devastating ways, which makes betting on them at the very least distasteful. But ethics aside, there is also a national security risk. Prediction markets can create incentives to leak classified information as in the case of the capture of Maduro. And the concern goes further, these markets don't just predict events, they could influence decision-making. Imagine a politician deciding on the possibility of military action while knowing that one outcome could lead to large profits on a prediction market. In that scenario, decisions affecting millions of lives aren't driven solely by the public interest. They are tied to financial bets, and that inevitably brings us to how these markets are regulated. Several countries have already banned prediction markets under gambling laws. Platforms argue this is the wrong classification, claiming they are financial markets, not gambling. In the United States, the Trump administration has been relatively favorable toward prediction markets. They are regulated at the federal level by the CFTC, since events contracts are treated as financial derivatives. But regulation remains complicated, the CFTC prohibits contracts tied to war, terrorism or assassinations. So when Iran's supreme leader was killed last weekend, Kalshi settled its related market based on the price just before his death, instead of paying everyone the full winnings. Even though that was part of the market terms, many users were upset by how it was handled. Polymarket operates offshore on blockchain infrastructure, which makes enforcement difficult even when restrictions exist. In the US, a new bill aims to restrict officials from using prediction markets. That may not be enough to address national security risks, because insiders are not only elected officials. That's why some argue that certain categories of events should be excluded from prediction markets entirely. So here is our takeaway. Prediction markets are clearly here to stay, and in our view, they are not just a form of gambling. In the right circumstances, they can serve a real public purpose, offering relatively accurate and timely insights into the likelihood of future events. At the same time, these markets still operate in a regulatory gray area. That creates real challenges around consumer protection, but also ethical and security concerns that haven't been addressed yet. Looking ahead, we expect stronger and clearer rules to shape how prediction markets operate. And now we'd love to hear from you. Have you used prediction markets?
